concepts.title: Nucleotide Anatomy and the Polynucleotide Chain

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Nucleotide Anatomy and the Polynucleotide Chain' refers to.
questions.a: A nucleotide assembles from three parts -- a nitrogenous base, a five-carbon sugar and a phosphate group; base plus sugar forms a nucleoside through an N-glycosidic bond, adding phosphate builds the nucleotide, and 3'-5' phosphodiester bonds string nucleotides into a chain whose backbone is sugar-phosphate with the bases jutting outward.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Nucleotide Anatomy and the Polynucleotide Chain'.
questions.a: Sugar type and base identity are the only switches separating dna building blocks from rna ones -- deoxyribose versus ribose, thymine versus uracil.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Nucleotide Anatomy and the Polynucleotide Chain' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 5.1.1 (source: lebo105.txt lines 60-98 (polynucleotide chain chemistry, DNA length examples))

concepts.title: Watson-Crick Double Helix and Base Pairing

questions.q: How many hydrogen bonds join adenine to thymine and guanine to cytosine? Use the method 'Watson-Crick Double Helix and Base Pairing'. Work with: helix_pitch = 3.4. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of helix_pitch.
questions.a: 3.4 units

questions.q: How many base pairs fit into one complete turn of the dna helix? Use the method 'Watson-Crick Double Helix and Base Pairing'. Work with: helix_pitch = 3.4. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of helix_pitch.
questions.a: 3.4 units

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Watson-Crick Double Helix and Base Pairing' refers to.
questions.a: Two antiparallel sugar-phosphate strands coil right-handedly around a common axis; inside, adenine faces thymine over two hydrogen bonds and guanine faces cytosine over three, so a purine always opposes a pyrimidine, the strands hold an even gap, and roughly ten base pairs fill each 3.4 nm turn of the helix.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Watson-Crick Double Helix and Base Pairing'.
questions.a: Complementarity is the master stroke -- either strand predicts its partner, exactly what a heritable molecule needs for faithful copying.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Watson-Crick Double Helix and Base Pairing', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: helix_pitch = 3.4

concepts.title: The Search for Genetic Material: Griffith to Hershey-Chase

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'The Search for Genetic Material: Griffith to Hershey-Chase' refers to.
questions.a: Griffith watched harmless bacteria turn lethal after mingling with heat-killed virulent ones and credited an unknown transforming principle; Avery, MacLeod and McCarty pinned the principle to dna by digesting each candidate in turn, and Hershey and Chase closed the case with radiolabelled phages whose phosphorus-tagged dna -- never their sulfur-tagged protein -- slipped into the bacteria.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'The Search for Genetic Material: Griffith to Hershey-Chase'.
questions.a: Three experiments in a row narrowed the answer from something to protein-versus-dna to dna alone.

questions.q: Under which section is 'The Search for Genetic Material: Griffith to Hershey-Chase' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 5.2 (source: lebo105.txt lines 228-299 (Griffith 1928, Avery-MacLeod-McCarty 1933-44, Hershey-Chase 1952))

concepts.title: DNA versus RNA as Genetic Material and the RNA World

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'DNA versus RNA as Genetic Material and the RNA World' refers to.
questions.a: A genetic molecule must copy itself, keep its structure, admit slow mutation and be expressible; dna outscores rna on stability because it drops the reactive 2' hydroxyl and swaps uracil for thymine, while rna's restlessness suits messenger, adapter and catalytic jobs -- clues that rna ran the earliest cells and dna was refined out of it later.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'DNA versus RNA as Genetic Material and the RNA World'.
questions.a: Storage favours the stable molecule (dna), dynamic messaging and catalysis favour the reactive one (rna) -- and life very likely began in an rna-only world.

questions.q: Under which section is 'DNA versus RNA as Genetic Material and the RNA World' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 5.2.2, 5.3 (source: lebo105.txt lines 301-375 (criteria for genetic material, stability argument, RNA world))

concepts.title: Replication Machinery: Enzymes, Fork and Origin

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Replication Machinery: Enzymes, Fork and Origin' refers to.
questions.a: dna-dependent dna polymerase lengthens chains only in the 5'-to-3' direction, so one template is read continuously while its partner is copied in short pieces that dna ligase later seals; unwinding happens locally at the replication fork, initiation occurs only at special origins, and the deoxynucleoside triphosphate substrates bankroll the reaction with their own high-energy phosphates.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Replication Machinery: Enzymes, Fork and Origin'.
questions.a: One-directional polymerisation forces the asymmetric fork -- a continuous leading side and a discontinuous, ligase-stitched lagging side.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Replication Machinery: Enzymes, Fork and Origin' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 5.4.2 (source: lebo105.txt lines 441-491 (polymerase, rate ~2000 bp/s, replication fork, ligase, origin, S-phase))

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Transcription Unit: Promoter, Gene, Terminator' refers to.
questions.a: A transcription unit stretches from a promoter, through the structural gene, to a terminator; only one strand is copied -- the 3'-to-5' template -- while its partner, matching the rna letter-for-letter except for thymine, oddly gets the name coding strand, and which strand plays which role is decided purely by where the promoter sits.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Transcription Unit: Promoter, Gene, Terminator'.
questions.a: Copying both strands would make complementary rnas that anneal into a dead double strand -- so one strand, one direction, sharply marked boundaries.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Transcription Unit: Promoter, Gene, Terminator' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 5.5, 5.5.1 (source: lebo105.txt lines 492-552 (definition of transcription, why one strand, unit boundaries, strand conventions))

concepts.title: RNA Polymerases, Split Genes and mRNA Processing

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'RNA Polymerases, Split Genes and mRNA Processing' refers to.
questions.a: Bacteria run all rna synthesis through a single polymerase that starts with a sigma factor and stops with rho, whereas eukaryotes divide the labour among three polymerases and must edit their interrupted genes -- splicing introns out of exons, capping the 5' end and tailing the 3' end -- before the finished mrna may leave the nucleus.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'RNA Polymerases, Split Genes and mRNA Processing'.
questions.a: Split genes and rna editing are living traces of the rna world; bacteria skip the editing because transcription and translation share one compartment.

questions.q: Under which section is 'RNA Polymerases, Split Genes and mRNA Processing' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 5.5.2, 5.5.3 (source: lebo105.txt lines 553-638 (cistron, exons/introns, three RNA types, bacterial vs eukaryotic transcription, splicing/capping/tailing))

concepts.title: The Genetic Code: Triplet, Degenerate, Universal

questions.q: How many codons specify amino acids and how many act as stop signals? Use the method 'The Genetic Code: Triplet, Degenerate, Universal'. Work with: codon_length = 5, base_types = 4. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of codon_count.
questions.a: 1024 units

questions.q: Work out how many codons four bases can generate in groups of three. Use the method 'The Genetic Code: Triplet, Degenerate, Universal'. Work with: codon_length = 3, base_types = 4. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of codon_count.
questions.a: 64 units

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'The Genetic Code: Triplet, Degenerate, Universal' refers to.
questions.a: Three nucleotide letters per codon is the shortest scheme letting four bases spell all twenty amino acids -- four cubed yields 64 codons, sixty-one with meanings and three stop signals; the message reads continuously with no punctuation, holds nearly unchanged from bacteria to humans, doubles aug as methionine codon and start signal, and keeps multiple synonyms for most amino acids.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'The Genetic Code: Triplet, Degenerate, Universal'.
questions.a: Degeneracy cushions point mutations -- with several synonyms per amino acid, a single-base error often swaps in a harmless synonym.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'The Genetic Code: Triplet, Degenerate, Universal', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: codon_count = base_types ** codon_length

concepts.title: Frameshift Mutations and the Reading Frame

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Frameshift Mutations and the Reading Frame' refers to.
questions.a: Inserting or deleting one or two bases knocks every downstream codon out of register because the three-letter reading frame slips, while adding or removing three bases -- or any multiple of three -- merely adds or drops whole amino acids and leaves the remainder of the message intact.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Frameshift Mutations and the Reading Frame'.
questions.a: The three-letter-word sentence analogy shows why only multiples of three keep a gene's message readable.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Frameshift Mutations and the Reading Frame' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 5.6.1 (source: lebo105.txt lines 702-739 (point mutation recap, RAM HAS RED CAP frameshift analogy))

concepts.title: Translation: tRNA, Ribosome and Polypeptide Synthesis

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Translation: tRNA, Ribosome and Polypeptide Synthesis' refers to.
questions.a: Amino acids have no way of reading codons themselves, so trna adapters each pick up their own amino acid and match their anticodon loop to the mrna message; the ribosome then welds the cargo together -- its 23s rrna even catalyses the peptide bond -- marching from the aug start codon until a release factor meets a stop codon and frees the finished polypeptide.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Translation: tRNA, Ribosome and Polypeptide Synthesis'.
questions.a: Every peptide bond costs energy, paid up front when atp charges each trna with its amino acid.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Translation: tRNA, Ribosome and Polypeptide Synthesis' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 5.6.2, 5.7 (source: lebo105.txt lines 740-815 (tRNA adapter, charging, ribosome structure, UTRs, translation phases))

concepts.title: Lac Operon: Negative Regulation by an Inducer

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Lac Operon: Negative Regulation by an Inducer' refers to.
questions.a: The lac operon of Jacob and Monod bundles a repressor gene (i) with three lactose-processing genes (z, y, a) under one promoter; the constitutively made repressor parks on the operator and blocks transcription until lactose, acting as inducer, disarms it -- so beta-galactosidase, permease and transacetylase appear only when the sugar is actually available.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Lac Operon: Negative Regulation by an Inducer'.
questions.a: A substrate switching on the enzymes that digest it is the classic case of negative control in bacteria.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Lac Operon: Negative Regulation by an Inducer' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 5.8, 5.8.1 (source: lebo105.txt lines 816-898 (levels of regulation, operon concept, i/z/y/a genes, inducer mechanism))

concepts.title: Human Genome Project: Goals, Methods and Findings

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Human Genome Project: Goals, Methods and Findings' refers to.
questions.a: Launched in 1990 and wrapped up in 2003, the human genome project read all three billion base pairs using expressed sequence tags plus blind whole-genome sequencing cloned into bacterial or yeast artificial chromosomes, automated sanger-style reads and computer assembly; it settled on roughly twenty thousand to twenty-five thousand genes and revealed that repeats dominate the genome.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Human Genome Project: Goals, Methods and Findings'.
questions.a: Under two percent of the genome codes for protein, chromosome 1 carries the most genes and the y the fewest, and snp mapping transformed the hunt for disease loci.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Human Genome Project: Goals, Methods and Findings' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 5.9 (source: lebo105.txt lines 903-1055 (mega project scale, goals, EST vs annotation, salient features, applications))

concepts.title: DNA Fingerprinting: Satellite DNA, VNTR and Uses

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'DNA Fingerprinting: Satellite DNA, VNTR and Uses' refers to.
questions.a: Tandemly repeated satellite sequences scattered through the genome code for no protein yet differ enormously in repeat count from person to person; Alec Jeffreys exploited these variable mini-satellites as probes -- isolate, digest, separate, blot, hybridise, autoradiograph -- yielding a band pattern unique to everyone except identical twins, the foundation of forensic and paternity testing.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'DNA Fingerprinting: Satellite DNA, VNTR and Uses'.
questions.a: Repetitive non-coding dna accumulates variation freely because changes there rarely harm reproduction, which is what makes each person's band pattern personal.

questions.q: Under which section is 'DNA Fingerprinting: Satellite DNA, VNTR and Uses' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 5.10 (source: lebo105.txt lines 1056-1151 (satellite vs bulk DNA, polymorphism definition, VNTR technique steps, applications))
